scenes.tts: Your body dismantles roughly two hundred fifty grams of protein daily. Why spend A T P to destroy what the cell already built? Follow one protein through a recycling center, where selection matters more than demolition.
scenes.caption: Your body dismantles roughly 250 grams of protein daily. Why spend ATP to destroy what the cell already built? Follow one protein through a recycling center, where selection matters more than demolition.
scenes.visual: Open inside one persistent, full-frame schematic cellular recycling center. A wide conveyor carries a large flexible train of rounded blocks labelled 'one protein' toward a closed sorting gate; bins labelled 'reuse' and 'burn' turn slowly in the distance. During the first sentence, a counter above the conveyor rolls to 'roughly 250 g/day' as many faint block trains pass behind the main one. On the question, a gold ATP token circles the locked gate while a large question mark rises from it. During 'Follow,' the camera tracks the main protein toward the gate and the title 'Choose, Recycle, Split' writes overhead. Belts, rollers, and small background block trains move throughout. Everything is labelled 'schematic'; draw no molecular structure.
scenes.narration: Your body dismantles roughly 250 grams of protein daily. Why spend ATP to destroy what the cell already built? Follow one protein through a recycling center, where selection matters more than demolition.

scenes.tts: Proteins have different expiration dates. Some last minutes; others last months or a lifetime. Turnover removes damaged proteins and changes signals. Yet peptide-bond hydrolysis is downhill. What is A T P buying?
scenes.caption: Proteins have different expiration dates. Some last minutes; others last months or a lifetime. Turnover removes damaged proteins and changes signals. Yet peptide-bond hydrolysis is downhill. What is ATP buying?
scenes.visual: Carry the same main protein along the conveyor. Three large clock faces marked 'minutes,' 'months,' and 'lifetime' roll past above it at different speeds; the protein's route switches between them as each duration is named. On 'removes damaged proteins,' one visibly dented labelled block train is diverted into the center; on 'changes signals,' a bright signal lamp switches off when a second labelled block train is diverted. On 'downhill,' a short ramp labelled 'peptide-bond hydrolysis' tilts downward beside the still-locked gate, and the ATP token hovers above it without falling in. End with the question mark enlarging while conveyor rollers continue turning. Keep no more than the three clocks, main protein, gate, and ATP token prominent.
scenes.narration: Proteins have different expiration dates. Some last minutes; others last months or a lifetime. Turnover removes damaged proteins and changes signals. Yet peptide-bond hydrolysis is downhill. What is ATP buying?

scenes.tts: Ubiquitin is the address label. E one spends A T P to activate it. E two carries it. An E three ligase recognizes the target and applies the tag. Hundreds of E threes create selectivity. A classic lysine-forty-eight chain sends the protein toward the proteasome.
scenes.caption: Ubiquitin is the address label. E1 spends ATP to activate it. E2 carries it. An E3 ligase recognizes the target and applies the tag. Hundreds of E3s create selectivity. A classic K48 chain sends the protein toward the proteasome.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the same sorting gate, keeping the reuse and burn exits visible behind it. Before 'ubiquitin,' a small gold badge settles beside the main protein; then the label 'ubiquitin' appears on the badge. On 'E one,' an E1-shaped activation dock cracks one ATP token into AMP plus a pyrophosphate chip and lights the badge. On 'E two,' a moving E2 cart carries that same badge to a large E3 clamp. On 'recognizes,' the E3 clamp tests the main protein's matching target notch and presses the badge onto it. A fan of faint E3 clamp silhouettes scrolls behind the chosen clamp during 'Hundreds.' Finally, four gold badges join into a chain marked 'K48' and the gate swings toward a large proteasome machine. Use labelled mechanical cartoons only, never molecular structures.
scenes.narration: Ubiquitin is the address label. E1 spends ATP to activate it. E2 carries it. An E3 ligase recognizes the target and applies the tag. Hundreds of E3s create selectivity. A classic K48 chain sends the protein toward the proteasome.

scenes.tts: Predict where energy goes. Does A T P power peptide-bond cutting, or pay for something else? Hold your answer as the tagged protein reaches the machine.
scenes.caption: Predict where energy goes. Does ATP power peptide-bond cutting, or pay for something else? Hold your answer as the tagged protein reaches the machine.
scenes.visual: The tagged protein travels from the sorting gate toward the large proteasome machine on the same conveyor. Two answer panels grow beside the path: 'cut bonds?' above a closed cutter icon and 'something else?' above an empty gear. A gold ATP token moves back and forth between the panels without choosing. The question stays large across the upper third, while the conveyor and machine rollers keep moving and the tagged protein advances slowly but does not enter.
scenes.narration: Predict where energy goes. Does ATP power peptide-bond cutting, or pay for something else? Hold your answer as the tagged protein reaches the machine.

scenes.visual: Hold the exact prediction layout for 4.5 seconds. Keep both answer panels and the question visible. The ATP token continues moving between the two choices, a circular thinking timer traces one turn, the conveyor creeps forward, and the tagged protein stops just outside the proteasome. Reveal no answer.

scenes.tts: Not to cutting. The proteasome's regulatory cap recognizes the tag, then uses A T P to unfold and thread the protein. The core cuts it into short peptides without A T P. Deubiquitinases recover the tag. Energy buys choice and controlled handling, not favorable bond hydrolysis.
scenes.caption: Not to cutting. The proteasome's regulatory cap recognizes the tag, then uses ATP to unfold and thread the protein. The core cuts it into short peptides without ATP. Deubiquitinases recover the tag. Energy buys choice and controlled handling, not favorable bond hydrolysis.
scenes.visual: Resolve the prediction within the same machine. The 'cut bonds?' panel dims and its ATP slot closes. On 'regulatory cap,' the bright cap reads the moving K48 badge chain; ATP tokens turn cap gears that pull the rounded protein blocks into a single-file strand and thread it inward. At the cap entrance, before the strand enters the core, a small recycling arm removes the gold badges and, on 'Deubiquitinases,' sends them back toward the sorting gate; no badge enters the core. Inside the core, concealed cutters move as short peptide block groups exit, but no ATP enters the core. During the final sentence, transform the ATP token into two large moving gears labelled 'choose' and 'handle,' while the downhill hydrolysis ramp remains unpowered.
scenes.narration: Not to cutting. The proteasome's regulatory cap recognizes the tag, then uses ATP to unfold and thread the protein. The core cuts it into short peptides without ATP. Deubiquitinases recover the tag. Energy buys choice and controlled handling, not favorable bond hydrolysis.

scenes.tts: Peptidases release amino acids into a shared pool. In an adult at nitrogen balance, most return to protein. The surplus is burned. The cell selects proteins, reuses most products, then separates surplus amino acids by atom.
scenes.caption: Peptidases release amino acids into a shared pool. In an adult at nitrogen balance, most return to protein. The surplus is burned. The cell selects proteins, reuses most products, then separates surplus amino acids by atom.
scenes.visual: Follow the short peptide block groups from the proteasome into a peptidase station, where they separate into individual amino-acid tiles. The tiles circulate through a large central pool labelled 'amino acids.' On 'most return,' a broad stream of tiles loops through the reuse bin and assembles into new labelled protein block trains. On 'surplus,' a narrower stream diverts toward the burn lane; label the scope above the pool 'adult · nitrogen balance.' As the guiding sentence is spoken, the sorting gate, broad reuse loop, and narrow burn lane glow in order while all three continue moving.
scenes.narration: Peptidases release amino acids into a shared pool. In an adult at nitrogen balance, most return to protein. The surplus is burned. The cell selects proteins, reuses most products, then separates surplus amino acids by atom.

scenes.tts: In this simplest adult human picture, each burned amino acid poses two problems. Nitrogen can be toxic; carbon remains valuable. Nitrogen passes onto glutamate and often through alanine or glutamine in blood. The carbon skeleton moves toward central metabolism.
scenes.caption: In this simplest adult human picture, each burned amino acid poses two problems. Nitrogen can be toxic; carbon remains valuable. Nitrogen passes onto glutamate and often through alanine or glutamine in blood. The carbon skeleton moves toward central metabolism.
scenes.visual: Stay on the narrow burn lane and enlarge one amino-acid tile. A mechanical fork separates it into a gold token labelled 'nitrogen' and a blue block labelled 'carbon skeleton'; mark the fork 'schematic.' On 'toxic,' the gold token makes a danger gauge rise, while the blue block lights a value gauge; both gauges are marked 'schematic.' During 'passes,' the gold token moves hand-to-hand across labelled carrier carts: glutamate first, still inside the tissue, then two branching carts labelled alanine and glutamine that roll out into a wide blood lane. At the same time, the blue carbon block travels on a parallel lower conveyor toward a distant central-metabolism hub. Keep both paths moving for the entire scene.
scenes.narration: In this simplest adult human picture, each burned amino acid poses two problems. Nitrogen can be toxic; carbon remains valuable. Nitrogen passes onto glutamate and often through alanine or glutamine in blood. The carbon skeleton moves toward central metabolism.

scenes.tts: In the liver, most waste nitrogen is packaged as urea. One urea nitrogen comes from ammonium; the other comes from aspartate. The cycle spends four high-energy phosphate bonds per urea. It converts a dangerous load into an excretable product.
scenes.caption: In the liver, most waste nitrogen is packaged as urea. One urea nitrogen comes from ammonium; the other comes from aspartate. The cycle spends four high-energy phosphate bonds per urea. It converts a dangerous load into an excretable product.
scenes.visual: Track the gold nitrogen token into a large liver-shaped recycling room connected to the same blood lane. A five-station wheel labelled 'urea cycle' turns continuously. On 'One urea nitrogen,' one gold token arrives on an ammonium cart; on 'the other,' a second arrives on an aspartate cart. The two tokens ride the turning wheel and leave together inside one capsule labelled 'urea.' During the energy sentence, four small high-energy-bond marks tick down beside the wheel without drawing ATP molecules. Finally, the danger gauge falls as urea capsules move into an excretion chute. Keep the wheel, incoming carts, and outgoing capsules moving; all chemistry remains schematic.
scenes.narration: In the liver, most waste nitrogen is packaged as urea. One urea nitrogen comes from ammonium; the other comes from aspartate. The cycle spends four high-energy phosphate bonds per urea. It converts a dangerous load into an excretable product.

scenes.tts: Carbon skeletons enter through seven metabolic doors. Five can supply net glucose because they can become oxaloacetate. The acetyl coenzyme A and acetoacetyl coenzyme A doors cannot. Only leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic.
scenes.caption: Carbon skeletons enter through seven metabolic doors. Five can supply net glucose because they can become oxaloacetate. The acetyl-CoA and acetoacetyl-CoA doors cannot. Only leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic.
scenes.visual: Return to the blue carbon block on its parallel conveyor and let it reach a large central-metabolism hub with one rotating doorway. During 'seven metabolic doors,' numbered cards one through seven pass through that doorway sequentially as a counter rises to seven. On 'Five,' five blue cards stack beside one path flowing through an oxaloacetate roundabout to a glucose exit; the counter reads '5 can yield net glucose.' The remaining two cards rotate forward and receive labels 'acetyl-CoA' and 'acetoacetyl-CoA'; their shared path turns toward ketone and fat storage icons, never the glucose exit. On the last sentence, a leucine tile travels only through those two labelled cards and a lysine tile only through 'acetoacetyl-CoA.' Keep the doorway, counter, and both grouped paths moving; label the map 'schematic.'
scenes.narration: Carbon skeletons enter through seven metabolic doors. Five can supply net glucose because they can become oxaloacetate. The acetyl-CoA and acetoacetyl-CoA doors cannot. Only leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic.

scenes.tts: Now the recycling center's logic is visible. Select the protein before dismantling it. Reuse most amino acids. When surplus is burned, cage its nitrogen and keep its carbon in metabolism. Choose what dies, recycle most, then split surplus amino acids by atom.
scenes.caption: Now the recycling center's logic is visible. Select the protein before dismantling it. Reuse most amino acids. When surplus is burned, cage its nitrogen and keep its carbon in metabolism. Choose what dies, recycle most, then split surplus amino acids by atom.
scenes.visual: Zoom back through the entire persistent recycling center. The tagged-protein sorting gate works at left, the broad amino-acid reuse loop circulates in the center, and the narrow burn fork sends gold nitrogen toward the turning urea wheel and blue carbon toward the seven-door hub at right. Illuminate those four actions in spoken order: select, dismantle, reuse, split. On the final rule, transform the moving layout into three large connected icons that still animate: a sorting gate marked 'choose,' a circular arrow marked 'recycle most,' and a fork marked 'split surplus.' Keep the urea wheel and seven-door hub moving faintly behind them.
scenes.narration: Now the recycling center's logic is visible. Select the protein before dismantling it. Reuse most amino acids. When surplus is burned, cage its nitrogen and keep its carbon in metabolism. Choose what dies, recycle most, then split surplus amino acids by atom.

scenes.visual: End card on the same dark ground. Hex waves above the line 'Choose what dies, recycle most, then split surplus amino acids by atom.' The sorting-gate, circular-reuse, and split-fork icons drift gently beneath the line; do not repeat the title.
